entries.label: About
entries.value: Aniwhenua is the middle of three hydro schemes on the Rangitāiki River in the eastern Bay of Plenty, between Murupara and Whakatāne. A 10 m barrage above the Aniwhenua Falls turns the river into a 2.2 km concrete-lined canal and a head pond, from which two buried penstocks feed the power station beside the falls. The Bay of Plenty Electric Power Board built it under a government scheme of the late 1970s that helped local bodies develop small hydro, and it began generating in October 1980. Nova Energy owned it from 1998 until 2016, when it passed to a partnership that Pioneer Energy has wholly owned since 2024.

entries.value: Aratiatia is 13 km downstream of Taupō on the Waikato River and has the smallest reservoir in the Waikato Hydro System. Its dam was built at the top of the Aratiatia gorge rather than the bottom, so the rapids could be kept, and water is let through to flood them several times a day for visitors. The station opened in 1964 with three Francis turbines.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Aviemore was approved in October 1962 and fully running by 1968, completing the mid-Waitaki scheme with Benmore upstream and Waitaki below. Its dam is built in two parts, one of earth and one of concrete. The station's four 55 MW generators are physically the largest in New Zealand, with rotors almost 8 m across weighing 210 tonnes, and its 7 m penstocks are also the country's largest.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Benmore holds back Lake Benmore, New Zealand's largest artificial lake, behind the country's largest earth dam; it was first planned in concrete, like Waitaki. Approved in October 1957 together with the Cook Strait power cable, it was built from 1958, the lake filled in December 1964 and the first power came in January 1965. It is New Zealand's second-largest hydro station after Manapōuri, and Meridian raised its maximum operating capacity to 570 MW in July 2026.

entries.label: About
entries.value: The Branch River scheme, in the Wairau Valley in inland Marlborough, is a run-of-river scheme with two power stations. Water taken from the Branch River runs along a race to the Argyle powerhouse, then through a storage pond, Lake Argyle, and a second race to the Wairau powerhouse, which discharges into the Wairau River. The Marlborough Electric Power Board built it, gaining the government's consent to generate in March 1983. Lake Argyle and the Branch and Leatham rivers are popular with anglers.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Clyde holds back Lake Dunstan on the Clutha River and is New Zealand's largest concrete gravity dam, with about a million cubic metres of concrete in the dam and another 200,000 in the powerhouse. The government chose a high dam at Clyde in 1976 and passed special legislation in 1982 to get it built. The dam was finished in 1990, but extensive work to stabilise the Cromwell Gorge, which the lake would fill, held up commissioning until 1992. Built to produce 432 MW from its four units, the station is now rated at 464 MW.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Cobb stands where the Cobb River meets the Tākaka, on the edge of Kahurangi National Park in Golden Bay. Its water falls almost 600 m from the storage lake to the powerhouse, the greatest head of any power station in New Zealand, so a small flow makes a lot of power. A private company planned the scheme in the 1930s but could not raise the money; the government took it over, first power came in 1944, and a storage dam was finished in 1954. Until 1955, when a line from Stoke joined the region to the South Island grid, Cobb supplied Nelson and Tasman on its own.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Coleridge, in inland Canterbury, was the New Zealand Government's first major hydro scheme, built from 1911, largely by hand, to supply Christchurch, and running from 1914. It needs no dam: Lake Coleridge is a natural lake about 165 m above the powerhouse, and its water reaches the turbines through tunnels and steel penstocks, then flows into the Rakaia River. Diversions of the Harper, Acheron and Wilberforce rivers later added water to the lake. Five units run today, after a refurbishment finished in 2008.

entries.label: About
entries.value: This cogeneration plant supplies process steam and electricity to Fonterra's Whareroa dairy site near Hāwera, one of the largest dairy processing sites in the Southern Hemisphere. Its main job is steam: four gas turbines each feed a heat recovery boiler, and the steam drives a steam turbine or goes to the factory, so electricity is a co-product. Running since 1996, it was a Fonterra and Todd joint venture until Fonterra took full ownership in August 2026. Fonterra is adding two 34 MW electric boilers, but the site still needs the plant for the rest of its heat.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Highbank, on the south bank of the Rakaia River in mid Canterbury, runs on water from the Rangitata Diversion Race, a canal built for irrigation: in summer farms have first call on the water, so the station generates mostly in winter. The Public Works Department built it alongside the race, and it opened in June 1945 with a single generator, then the largest in New Zealand. Since 2010 pumps at the site can lift water from the Rakaia back up the penstock into the race for irrigators. The 1945 unit is now being replaced, and the pumps have been run as small turbines in the meantime.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Huntly, on the Waikato River, is New Zealand's largest power station by capacity, and its Rankine units are its original part. Built as four 250 MW steam units able to burn either gas or coal, they were commissioned between 1982 and 1985. One unit was decommissioned in 2014 and three remain, run for baseload, to back up the hydro lakes in dry years, and for peaks. Genesis had planned to retire one of them in early 2026; in November 2025 the Commerce Commission authorised an arrangement under which Mercury, Meridian and Contact share its costs, keeping it available to the end of 2035.

entries.value: Junction Road is a 100 MW gas-fired peaking plant about 7 km south of New Plymouth, near State Highway 3. Built by Todd Generation, it went into commercial operation in May 2020, and Nova Energy took over its operation in 2022.

entries.label: About
entries.value: The Kaimai scheme gathers water from the Wairoa River and its tributaries on the Bay of Plenty side of the Kaimai Range and runs it through small storage lakes, canals and tunnels to four power stations. It grew out of Tauranga's own electricity undertakings: a joint committee of the city and the power board built Lloyd Mandeno, named after the engineer who brought electricity to the district, in 1972, then Lower Mangapapa in 1979 and Ruahihi in 1981. Releases from the Lake McLaren dam on up to 26 days a year give white-water kayakers and rafters high flows.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Kaiwaikawe Wind Farm is 12 km north-west of Dargaville in Northland and 3 km inland from the Tasman Sea, with its 12 turbines in two clusters. entries.label: About
entries.value: Karāpiro is the last station in the Waikato Hydro System, 188 km downstream of Lake Taupō near Cambridge, and its lake is home to New Zealand rowing. Building began in 1940 but was slowed by the Second World War, and its three Kaplan turbines came into service in 1947 and 1948. A $90 million upgrade, finished in September 2025, replaced all three units and raised the station from 96 MW to 112.5 MW.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Kawerau was New Zealand's biggest geothermal project in 20 years when Mighty River Power, now Mercury, opened it in 2008, on a field that has supplied steam to the town's mills since 1957. Fluid from wells about 2 km away is separated twice, giving high- and low-pressure steam for a single turbine, and the used fluid is injected back into the ground north of the field. Built for 90 MW, it soon proved able to run at about 100 MW, and Mercury now gives its installed capacity as 107 MW.

entries.value: The Kūmara scheme on the West Coast links three small power stations that have supplied the region since 1928: Duffers, Dillmans and Kūmara. Intakes on the Big Wainihinihi, the Arahura Wainihinihi and Kawhaka Creek collect water in the hills behind the scheme and send it down to Duffers; the Loopline and Kapitea reservoirs then supply Kūmara station. The sheltered Kapitea Reservoir is used for fishing, kayaking and power boating.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Manapōuri is New Zealand's largest hydro station, built in a cavern about 200 m below Lake Manapōuri's West Arm in Fiordland National Park. About 1,800 workers took eight years to build it: the first power came in September 1969 and all seven units were running by 1972. The water leaves through tailrace tunnels to Deep Cove in Doubtful Sound, and a second tunnel, finished in 2002, let the station reach its full rating, though its consent limits output to 800 MW. Plans in the 1960s to raise the lake by up to 30 m met wide public opposition, a landmark in New Zealand's environmental history.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Mangahao, near Shannon in Horowhenua, was the first North Island power station built by the government. Dams in the Tararua Range hold the Mangahao River's water, which runs through tunnels and pipelines to the powerhouse. The Prime Minister, William Massey, opened it in November 1924, after eight men had died building the tunnels, and its lines to Wellington, Palmerston North and Hawke's Bay became the start of the North Island grid. A joint venture of King Country Energy and Todd Energy bought it in 1997, and King Country Energy, now majority-owned by Contact Energy, has owned it outright since 2012.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Matahina's 86 m earth dam across the Rangitāiki River, inland from Whakatāne, is the largest dam of its kind in the North Island and holds back Lake Matahina. The Ministry of Works began the scheme in 1960 on difficult, faulted ground, and its two generators came into service in 1967. It is the lowest of the river's three hydro schemes, below Wheao and Flaxy and Aniwhenua. The Waiohau fault runs beneath the dam, which has since been strengthened against a large earthquake.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Mill Creek is in the hills above the Ōhāriu Valley, north-west of Wellington, on private farms whose owners chose wind farming over a housing subdivision or forestry and picked Meridian to build it. Building began in 2012, with about 800,000 cubic metres of earthworks and 19 km of tracks, and the 26 turbines (59.8 MW) were fully running in 2014, feeding the grid at Transpower's Wilton substation.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Mōkai, about 30 km northwest of Taupō, is majority-owned by the Tūaropaki Trust, with Mercury holding a quarter. It opened in 2000 as a 55 MW station and was enlarged in 2005 and again in 2007–08 to about 113 MW. It combines steam turbines with binary units, which make more electricity from the heat left in the fluid, and all the geothermal fluid goes back into the field. The field's heat also warms a large glasshouse and the Miraka milk-powder factory.

entries.label: About
entries.value: New Plymouth was a 600 MW station at Port Taranaki, New Zealand's first large thermal station planned to run continuously as baseload. It was designed for coal at first, then changed to burn natural gas or fuel oil after the Maui gas field was found. Its five units came into service between 1974 and 1976, and in later years it ran mostly in dry years. It was mothballed at the end of 2007, ran one unit through 2008's dry winter, and was demolished in 2014–15.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Ngā Awa Pūrua was built by Mighty River Power, now Mercury, in partnership with the Tauhara North No. 2 Trust, whose members are affiliated to Ngāti Tahu; the trust owns 35% of the station. It stands beside the older Rotokawa station on the Rotokawa field, 14 km northeast of Taupō, and its wells average 2,500 metres deep. Its single triple-flash steam turbine was at one time the largest geothermal turbine in the world, and it first generated in January 2010.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Ngā Tamariki, 17 km northeast of Taupō on the Wairakei Pastoral Estate, opened in 2013 with four Ormat binary units, at the time the largest of their kind in the world. In a binary plant the geothermal fluid heats a separate working fluid that drives the turbines, and the cooled fluid goes back into the reservoir. Ngā Tamariki also pumps its non-condensable gases, mostly carbon dioxide, back underground, which Mercury was the first New Zealand generator to do. A fifth unit, built from May 2024, began supplying the grid in January 2026 and lifted capacity from 86 MW to 132 MW.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Ōhaaki stands beside the Waikato River and the Ngāti Tahu marae of the same name, partly on land leased from its Māori owners, and was approved by the government in 1982. Opened on 31 October 1989, it was New Zealand's second geothermal power station and the first to put used geothermal fluid back into the ground. Its 105-metre concrete cooling tower, the first of its kind in the country, cools the condenser water so the river isn't used for cooling. Built for about 108 MW, it now produces much less: the steamfield has declined and one of its high-pressure turbines has been retired.

Building it meant digging about two million cubic metres of rock and gravel from the bank of the Ōhau River. Lake Ruataniwha, which feeds Ōhau B, has a national rowing course that began as the idea of the scheme's project engineer.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Ōtāhuhu A was the first power station on the Ōtāhuhu site in south Auckland, and the first large gas turbine station in Australia and New Zealand: four 45 MW open cycle gas turbines commissioned in 1968, joined by two more twin-pack units in 1978. The turbines burned fuel oil at first; the first was converted to natural gas from the Kapuni pipeline in 1971. It was returned to full operation during the 1992 power shortage. After it stopped generating in the late 1990s, its machines were kept running to supply reactive power to the national grid, until they were retired and decommissioned in 2013. Ōtāhuhu B, a combined cycle station, was built beside it.

entries.value: Papareireiā is a solar farm on farmland near Maungaturoto in the Kaipara, built to supply Ryman Healthcare's retirement villages under a 10-year agreement. It is a joint venture of Tupu Tonu (the Ngāpuhi Investment Fund), Purpose Capital and Harbour Infrastructure. Ryman's supply is sleeved through Mercury, which tops it up when the sun is low. entries.label: About
entries.value: Pātea's 82 m earth dam, the fourth highest in New Zealand, holds back Lake Rotorangi, which winds 46 km up the Pātea River valley in South Taranaki and is the country's longest man-made lake. Built between 1980 and 1984 for the Egmont Electric Power Board, it was the first dam made from soft sandstone and siltstone. The station helps eels both ways: a bypass and timed spillway openings for adults heading to sea, and a trap-and-transfer programme for young eels moving upstream.

entries.label: About
entries.value: The Roaring Meg scheme has two small stations in the Kawarau Gorge between Cromwell and Queenstown, fed from a dam on the Roaring Meg stream, which is said to be named after a gold-rush barmaid. The Otago Central Electric Power Board built the lower station with money advanced by two gold-dredging companies, and it opened in March 1936; workers drilled the rock by hand and hauled the pipes up the hill on a tramline. The upper station, below a concrete arch dam at the head of the valley, followed in 1947 despite wartime shortages, floods and snow.

entries.label: About
entries.value: The Stratford site east of Stratford has held three gas-fired stations. Four gas turbines ran here from 1976 until 2001; the Taranaki Combined Cycle unit, cooled with water from the Pātea River, ran from 1998 until it reached the end of its life in 2026; and two fast-start peakers, opened in 2011, remain. The peakers can go from a cold start to full output in about ten minutes, to cover peaks in demand and complement hydro and wind generation.

entries.value: Tauhara draws on the Tauhara geothermal field along the eastern edge of Taupō, and its single steam turbine is, Contact says, the largest single-shaft geothermal turbine in the world, spinning at 3,000 revolutions a minute. It first supplied the grid in May 2024 and was officially opened on 22 November 2024; at up to 174 MW it can meet around 3.5% of New Zealand's electricity needs.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Te Āpiti stands on farmland just north of the Manawatū Gorge, where the gap between the Ruahine and Tararua ranges funnels the westerly winds. Built from 2003 and fully running in 2004, it was Meridian's first wind farm and the first in New Zealand to connect straight to the national grid, through a 4.5 km line to Transpower's Woodville substation. Its 55 turbines can produce up to 90.75 MW; when they reached the end of their original design life in 2024, Meridian chose to extend their life rather than replace them.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Te Huka 3 is a binary plant built at Te Huka, on the Tauhara geothermal field near Taupō, beside the station's two original units. Geothermal fluid heats pentane, which drives the turbine, and the plant was designed to put all its potential emissions back into the reservoir, making it one of the first geothermal stations built to be carbon neutral. Microsoft agreed to buy its renewable energy attributes for ten years, which helped Contact decide to build it, and it first supplied the grid in October 2024.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Te Huka was the first power station on the Tauhara geothermal field, which lies east of the Waikato River from Wairākei, along the edge of Taupō. It is a binary plant: heat from the geothermal fluid boils a separate working fluid that drives the turbines, and the used geothermal fluid all goes back into the field. Its two units opened in 2010 and were upgraded in 2012, and a third, larger unit, Te Huka 3, was added at Te Huka in 2024.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Te Mihi draws steam from the western side of the Wairākei geothermal field, where the field's main upflow of hot fluid lies, and was built to take over gradually from the ageing Wairākei station nearby. Its two Toshiba steam turbines began generating in 2014; some of Wairākei's steam was moved to the new plant, so the field's total output rose. Contact is now building Te Mihi Stage 2, a 101 MW binary plant on the same field, due online in 2027 as the next step in replacing Wairākei.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Te Rapa was a gas-fired cogeneration plant at Fonterra's dairy factory at Te Rapa, near Hamilton, commissioned in 1999. Its gas turbine made electricity, and its exhaust heat raised steam for the factory. Plans for a 150 MW plant were cut to about 45 MW in 1997 after opposition over its emissions and the Waikato River. Contact closed it in 2023, when its contract to supply Fonterra ended.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Tekapo A stands at the southern end of Lake Tekapo, the first of the eight stations in the Waitaki hydro scheme. Work on it began in 1938 but stopped during the Second World War, and it opened in 1951. Its outflow now runs down the 25.5 km Tekapo Canal to Tekapo B, so the same water generates twice. Meridian Energy sold both Tekapo stations to Genesis Energy on 1 June 2011.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Tekapo B sits at the end of the 25.5 km Tekapo Canal on the edge of Lake Pūkaki, using water that has already passed through Tekapo A. It was built from 1970 and opened in 1977, before the Upper Waitaki works raised the lake around it; Genesis says it is the only New Zealand power station finished with water all around it. Its two 80 MW units make it the larger of the two Tekapo stations, which Genesis Energy bought from Meridian Energy in 2011.

entries.label: About
entries.value: The Teviot scheme in Central Otago carries water from Lake Onslow, high in the Lammerlaw Range, down the Teviot River through a chain of small dams and six power stations to the Clutha near Roxburgh. The first, George, opened in 1924; Bridge followed in 1972, then Ellis and Michelle in the early 1980s, when a new arch dam raised Lake Onslow, Horseshoe Bend in 1999 and Kowhai in 2010. Irrigation shares the water, and in summer it takes priority at some stations. Ellis runs on refurbished 1940s machinery bought from Dunedin's Waipori Falls station.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Turitea stands on the Tararua Range above Palmerston North, much of it in the city council's Turitea Reserve. The council chose Mercury, then Mighty River Power, to develop it in 2005, and after a long consent process a board of inquiry approved 60 turbines in 2011. The 33-turbine northern stage first generated in July 2021 and the 27-turbine southern stage followed; at 222 MW it was New Zealand's largest wind farm when it opened in May 2023. A 12 km, 220 kV line carries its power to Transpower's Linton substation.

entries.label: About
entries.value: The Waikaremoana Power Scheme in northern Hawke's Bay runs water from Lake Waikaremoana through three stations in turn: Kaitawa, Tuai and Piripaua. Tuai opened first, in 1929, making this the North Island's second government hydro scheme after Mangahao; Piripaua followed in 1943 and Kaitawa last. Kaitawa was the first to draw straight from the lake, through tunnels in the ancient landslide dam that formed it; before then the stations used only the water that leaked or spilled out. Tuai has the highest head and makes the largest share of the scheme's power.

entries.label: About
entries.value: The Waipori scheme, in the hills west of Dunedin, began as a private company's plan to power gold dredges. Dunedin City Council bought it while it was being built, in 1904, and power reached the city on 27 April 1907. Lake Mahinerangi, formed by a dam finished in 1931 and raised by 1946, now stores the water, which drops through a steep gorge to four stations. The council sold the scheme to TrustPower in 1998 under the electricity reforms. Elenz's figures for this plant cover Waipori 2A, 3 and 4, as the EA register groups them.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Wairākei was the world's second geothermal power station and the first to make electricity from wet steam, a mix of steam and hot water drawn from wells north of Taupō; the station stands beside the Waikato River. It began as a joint project with Britain's atomic energy authority to make heavy water as well as power, but the British withdrew in 1956 and the station was built for electricity alone: its first turbine ran in November 1958 and the B station was finished in 1963. A binary plant added in 2005 makes more power from heat left in the separated water. Contact plans to retire most of the station once Te Mihi Stage 2 is running, expected in 2027, and to close the rest by June 2031, when its resource consent ends.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Waitaki was the first station of the Waitaki scheme, begun in 1928 as a Depression "make work" project. Dug almost entirely by pick and shovel, it was the last New Zealand station built without modern machinery, and its first two 15 MW units, running from 1935, could meet nearly half the South Island's needs. Five more units followed by 1954. In 2026 Meridian began a $440–510 million upgrade, due by 2036, that will replace all seven and take the station from 105 MW to 120 MW.

entries.label: About
entries.value: West Wind stands on the coastal hills at Mākara, west of Wellington, where Cook Strait funnels strong, steady winds. Meridian began building it in 2007, bringing the turbine parts in through a temporary wharf at Oteranga Bay and 33 km of new roads to keep them off the city's streets. Its 62 turbines, up to 142.6 MW, were fully running in 2009, and a public recreation area lets visitors walk and bike among them.

It is also the main switching point for the upper Waikato's generation on its way north.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Wheao and Flaxy are two linked power stations in the Kaingaroa Forest, on the upper Rangitāiki River, the furthest upstream of the river's three hydro schemes. Three dams and two canals gather water from the Rangitāiki and Wheao rivers and Flaxy Stream for the two stations. The scheme was commissioned in 1982, and its Rangitāiki canal is now a good trout fishery.

entries.label: About
entries.value: Whirinaki, north of Napier, is a diesel-fired peaker plant. The government had it built after the power shortages of 2001 and 2003 as reserve generation of last resort, run by Contact Energy, and it opened in June 2004; Contact bought it in 2011. Its three fast-start units can reach full output from a cold start in 20 to 30 minutes, and about four million litres of diesel stored on site will run it at full output for 92 hours. An earlier gas turbine station on the same site ran from 1978 to 2001.

entries.label: About
entries.value: White Hill stands on forestry land south-east of Mossburn in Southland. It was Meridian's second wind farm and the first in the South Island: building began in 2006, and its 29 turbines, up to 58 MW, were fully running in 2007.
