iponz-get-ip-copyright-duration.note: NZ copyright duration guidance; old images can have transitional rules.

library-1983-1983-20issue-20071.title: New Zealand Gazette, 1983, issue 71: consent for the Marlborough Electric Power Board to generate electricity (Branch River Scheme)
library-1983-1983-20issue-20071.publisher: New Zealand Gazette (Victoria University of Wellington Library archive)
library-1983-1983-20issue-20071.note: Primary legal notice describes Argyle powerhouse at 3.8 MW and Wairau powerhouse at 7.2 MW, with associated waterworks.; Argyle: Legal notice gives 3.8 MW maximum capacity and describes turbine/generator and waterworks. Primary source for consented/authorised capacity; pair with current operator confirmation.; Wairau: Legal notice gives 7.2 MW maximum capacity and describes powerhouse downstream of Argyle. Likely related cascade; model scheme relationship to Argyle. Pages 1655–56; consent signed 29 March 1983.

mainpower-corporate-information-renewabl.title: MainPower – Renewable energy / Cleardale mini-hydro
mainpower-corporate-information-renewabl.note: Owner source for Cleardale mini-hydro; facility description and annual generation. Capacity needs confirmation.; Cleardale: Owner confirms mini-hydro facility, location near Mount Hutt and annual output about 4 GWh. MBIE lists 0.9 MW; below current 1 MW cutoff but a good embedded-generation example.

mbie-energy-statistics-renewables-statis.title: MBIE – Renewables statistics
mbie-energy-statistics-renewables-statis.note: All existing stations: Annual renewable energy workbook with hydro, wind, geothermal, solar, woody biomass and biogas tables. Useful for sector-level and some facility-level cross-checks; inspect workbook tabs and reporting basis.

mbie-new-zealand-2026-electricity.title: MBIE – Energy in NZ 2026: Electricity
mbie-new-zealand-2026-electricity.note: Generation and thermal/cogeneration context; may aggregate industrial generation.

mbie-new-zealand-2026-renewables.title: MBIE – Energy in NZ 2026: Renewables
mbie-new-zealand-2026-renewables.note: Renewable facility reporting; distinguish MWp/DC and MWac.

mbie-opportunities-in-new-zealand.title: MBIE – Embedded Hydro Generation Opportunities in New Zealand (2020)
mbie-opportunities-in-new-zealand.note: Appendix D lists 78 existing small hydro schemes, including 55 at >=1 MW; valuable independent cross-check for small/embedded hydro. Historical snapshot; verify current status and aliases.

mercury-arapuni.title: Arapuni Hydro Station
mercury-arapuni.note: Opened 1929; 8 Francis turbines (units 5-6 1938, 7-8 1946; 5-8 replaced 2012-13); 198 MW; 870 GWh a year.

mercury-aratiatia.title: Aratiatia Hydro Station
mercury-aratiatia.note: Opened 1964; 3 Francis turbines; 78 MW; 335 GWh a year; 13 km downstream of Taupō; rapids releases.

mercury-hydro.title: Hydro generation: the Waikato Hydro System
mercury-hydro.note: The nine Waikato River stations; planned upgrades (Ātiamuri 2031-34, Maraetai I 2030-34, Ōhakuri 2029-32).

mercury-karapiro.title: Karāpiro Hydro Station
mercury-karapiro.note: Built 1940-47; 3 Kaplan turbines of 37.5 MW, commissioned 1947-48; 112.5 MW since the upgrade completed Sep 2025 (96 MW before).

mercury-maraetai.title: Maraetai I and II Hydro Station
mercury-maraetai.note: Maraetai I opened 1952, Maraetai II 1970 (begun 1959, paused 1961); 5 Francis turbines and 180 MW each; one shared arch dam.

mercury-ohakuri.title: Ōhākurī Hydro Station
mercury-ohakuri.note: Opened 1961; 4 Francis turbines (replaced 2011-14); 112 MW; 405 GWh a year; Lake Ōhakuri 12 km².

mercury-waipapa.title: Waipāpa Hydro Station
mercury-waipapa.note: Opened 1961; 3 Kaplan turbines; 51 MW; 240 GWh a year; smallest station on the Waikato River.

mercury-whakamaru.title: Whakamaru Hydro Station
mercury-whakamaru.note: Built from 1949, operating 1956; 4 Francis turbines, replaced 2017-20; 124 MW; 515 GWh a year.

meridian-aviemore.title: Aviemore Power Station
meridian-aviemore.note: Four 55 MW units, up to 220 MW; generators the largest in NZ by size (rotors nearly 8 m, 210 t); earth and concrete dam; 7 m penstocks; approved October 1962; construction 1962, fully operational 1968; mid-Waitaki scheme with Benmore and Waitaki.

meridian-benmore.title: Benmore hydro station
meridian-benmore.note: Six 93 MW units, up to 552 MW (before the July 2026 reassessment); on Lake Benmore, NZ's largest artificial lake; NZ's largest earth dam; approved October 1957 with the Cook Strait cable; built from 1958; lake filled December 1964; first power January 1965.

meridian-hydro.title: Hydro stations
meridian-hydro.note: Waitaki hydro scheme: eight stations; Meridian owns and operates Aviemore, Benmore, Waitaki and Ōhau A, B and C; Genesis Energy owns and operates Tekapo A and B. Manapōuri is NZ's largest hydro station.

meridian-lake-levels.title: Lake levels
meridian-lake-levels.note: Lakes Pūkaki, Ōhau, Ruataniwha, Benmore, Aviemore, Waitaki, Manapōuri and Te Anau; flows in the Waitaki River below Benmore, Aviemore and Waitaki dams; Lakes Te Anau and Manapōuri supply Manapōuri.

meridian-manapouri.title: Manapōuri Power Station
meridian-manapouri.note: Seven 128 MW units; operating maximum 800 MW (consent), 850 MW maximum continuous rating with the second tailrace; cavern about 200 m below Lake Manapōuri (West Arm), Fiordland National Park; built from 1964 by about 1,800 workers over eight years; first power September 1969; fully operational 1972; second tailrace 1998–2002; tailraces to Deep Cove, Doubtful Sound.

meridian-ohau-a.title: Ōhau A Power Station
meridian-ohau-a.note: Four 66 MW units, up to 264 MW; at the end of the Pūkaki canal where it meets the Ōhau canal; third station of the Upper Waitaki scheme; construction 1971, fully operational 1979; Lake Ruataniwha rowing course.

meridian-ohau-b.title: Ōhau B hydro station
meridian-ohau-b.note: Four 53 MW units, up to 212 MW; twin of Ōhau C; water from Lake Ruataniwha into the Ōhau C canal; construction 1977, fully operational 1984.

meridian-ohau-c.title: Ōhau C Power Station
meridian-ohau-c.note: Twin of Ōhau B; four 53 MW units, up to 212 MW; outflow to Lake Benmore; construction 1979, fully operational 1985, the last station of the Waitaki scheme.

meridian-waitaki.title: Waitaki Power Station
meridian-waitaki.note: Seven 15 MW units, up to 105 MW; Depression make-work project, dug by pick and shovel; first two units 1935, three more 1940–49, last two 1952–54; $440–510 million upgrade to 120 MW, due by 2036.

meridian-waitaki-scheme.title: About the Waitaki hydro scheme
meridian-waitaki-scheme.note: Eight stations from Lake Tekapo to Lake Waitaki, six run by Meridian from Twizel; Waitaki dam begun 1928; Aviemore (1968) completed the mid-Waitaki scheme; Upper Waitaki 1968–85; 1999 Meridian assigned the scheme; 2011 Tekapo A and B sold to Genesis Energy.

meridian-waitaki-uprate.title: Increased generation capacity at Waitaki hydro stations (30 July 2026)
meridian-waitaki-uprate.note: Maximum operating capacity from 30 July 2026: Benmore 552 → 570 MW, Ōhau B 216 → 220 MW, Ōhau C 212 → 220 MW.

natlib-a-z-photographic-archive.title: National Library Photographic Archive
natlib-a-z-photographic-archive.note: Historic images; access does not imply reuse permission.

natlib-records-22657539.title: National Library of New Zealand – Hydroelectric power plants catalogue
natlib-records-22657539.note: Subject catalogue of historic hydroelectric power plant material; leads to archival photographs and records for named stations.

nzgeothermal-nz-what-is-geothermal.title: NZ Geothermal Association
nzgeothermal-nz-what-is-geothermal.note: Capacity and sector history; check gross/net basis.

nzx-announcements-376610.title: Mercury acquires Tilt Renewables' New Zealand operations (NZX, 3 August 2021)
nzx-announcements-376610.note: Mercury took ownership of Tilt's NZ operations on 3 Aug 2021: Tararua I, II and III, Mahinerangi and Waipipi, plus development options in Manawatū, Northland, Otago and Southland; Turitea first generated the week before.

nzx-mcy.title: Mercury NZ Limited (MCY): company page
nzx-mcy.note: Formerly Mighty River Power (NZX: MRP); renamed Mercury NZ Limited on 29 July 2016; listed May 2013.

nzx-meridian-waitaki-upgrade.title: Meridian to upgrade Waitaki Power Station (NZX, 29 September 2026)
nzx-meridian-waitaki-upgrade.note: $440–510 million over ten years; 105 MW to 120 MW by 2036; first two 15 MW units 1935, three more 1940–49, two more 1952–54.

openinframap-20zealand-plants-source-hyd.title: Open Infrastructure Map – NZ hydro plants
openinframap-20zealand-plants-source-hyd.note: Hydro-only inventory includes small stations and scheme components such as Argyle, Wairau, Ellis, Talla Burn, Kowhai and others. Check against operator evidence.

openinframap-area-new-20zealand-plants.title: Open Infrastructure Map – New Zealand power plants
openinframap-area-new-20zealand-plants.note: OSM-based independent mapped inventory; useful cross-check and discovery lead. Not authoritative; capacities and naming can be wrong or stale.

openstreetmap-copyright.title: OpenStreetMap – power=plant features in New Zealand (Overpass export, 8 Nov 2026)
openstreetmap-copyright.note: 158 features: station locations, Wikidata IDs, start dates; capacities and operators are often stale. © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL 1.0: attribution needed, and a database built from it that is shared publicly must also be ODbL.

openverse-en-nz-about.title: Openverse
openverse-en-nz-about.note: Openly licensed image search; verify original source licence.

osm.title: OpenStreetMap
osm.note: ODbL: research only. Its coordinates and other values are not copied into these files.

statsnz-regc-2025.title: Regional Council 2025 (boundaries)
statsnz-regc-2025.note: Region boundaries (CC BY 4.0). We test a station's point against them.

statsnz-ta-2026.title: Territorial Authority 2026 (boundaries)
statsnz-ta-2026.note: District boundaries (CC BY 4.0). We test a station's point against them.

trusthouse-korarau-hydroelectric-power-s.title: Trust House – Kourarau Hydroelectric Power Scheme
trusthouse-korarau-hydroelectric-power-s.note: Operator/owner source: two stations A and B, 700 kW + 250 kW, 910 kW combined, operating since 1923.; Kourarau A and B: Two stations; combined installed capacity 910 kW; 3 GWh/year; continuous operation since 1923. Strong owner source; use 0.91 MW combined rather than rounded 1 MW.

wd-q123943230.title: Wikidata item Q123943230
wd-q123943230.note: Tokaanu Power Station: coordinates; 240 MW; part of the Tongariro Power Scheme (Q12006578). Replaces Q61448287, which now redirects to the scheme item.

wd-q140119415.title: Wikidata item Q140119415
wd-q140119415.note: Piripaua Power Station: coordinates; inception 1943; 42 MW.

wd-q140121649.title: Wikidata item Q140121649
wd-q140121649.note: Kaitawa Power Station: coordinates; inception 1949; 36 MW.

wd-q61448285.title: Wikidata item Q61448285
wd-q61448285.note: Rangipo power station: coordinates; service entry 1983; 120 MW; part of the Tongariro Power Scheme (Q12006578).

wd-q61448290.title: Wikidata item Q61448290
wd-q61448290.note: Tuai Power Station: coordinates; inception 1929; 60 MW.

wd-query.title: Wikidata – items linked from OSM (SPARQL query, 8 Nov 2026)
wd-query.note: Coordinates (P625) and service entry / inception dates (P729, P571) for 59 stations. CC0: no conditions on reuse.

webstatic-library-tonlocal.title: NIWA – Hawke's Bay hydroelectric potential / Mokopeka report
webstatic-library-tonlocal.note: Historic regional technical report; records Mokopeka as about 20 kVA and includes 1978 photographs.; Mokopeka: About 20 kVA; photos of weir, powerhouse, turbine and pump taken in 1978. Useful technical/history and image lead; check image reuse rights.

windenergy-operating-onshore-windfarm-pr.title: NZ Wind Energy Association – Operating wind farms
windenergy-operating-onshore-windfarm-pr.note: Operating wind farms and indicative capacities; verify basis.

windenergy-wind-onshore-windfarm-pipelin.title: NZWEA – Wind pipeline
windenergy-wind-onshore-windfarm-pipelin.note: Proposed and staged projects; not commissioned capacity.

wp-aniwhenua-power-station.title: Aniwhenua Power Station
wp-aniwhenua-power-station.note: Bay of Plenty Electric Power Board scheme; began generating 3 October 1980; vested in Bay of Plenty Electricity August 1994; Nova Energy 1998; Southern Generation Partnership (Pioneer and Roaring Forties) from April 2016.

wp-arapuni.title: Arapuni Power Station
wp-arapuni.note: Infobox: creates Lake Arapuni; 8 Francis turbines; 196.66 MW.

wp-atiamuri.title: Ātiamuri Power Station
wp-atiamuri.note: Lake Ātiamuri; downstream of Ōhakuri and takes its water directly; first three units November 1958.

wp-aviemore-dam.title: Aviemore Dam
wp-aviemore-dam.note: Dam on the Waitaki River forming Lake Aviemore; 4 Francis turbines of 55 MW; 1962–68.

wp-list.title: List of power stations in New Zealand
wp-list.note: Read for the register (Nov 2026). Grade B: check each value against the station's own page or its references.; Station names, territorial authorities, coordinates, commissioning years, operators (read 8 Nov 2026). A lead, not evidence: check against operator pages.

wp-maraetai.title: Maraetai Power Station
wp-maraetai.note: Creates Lake Maraetai; two powerhouses operated as one station; 10 Francis turbines.

wp-ohakuri.title: Ōhakuri Dam
wp-ohakuri.note: Lake Ohakuri drowned two thirds of the Ōrākei Kōrako geothermal area.

wp-tekapo-a.title: Tekapo A Power Station
wp-tekapo-a.note: Southern end of Lake Tekapo; begun 1938, interrupted by the war, opened 1951; one unit, vertical Kaplan turbine, 30 MW; turbine destroyed 1986 and replaced; canal to Tekapo B; Meridian to 2011, then Genesis.

wp-tekapo-b.title: Tekapo B Power Station
wp-tekapo-b.note: Eastern shore of Lake Pūkaki; built 1970–77, before the lake was raised; two Francis units of 80 MW (citing Meridian's Discover the Waitaki Hydro Scheme); Meridian to 2011, then Genesis.

wp-waitaki-dam.title: Waitaki Dam
wp-waitaki-dam.note: Forms Lake Waitaki on the Waitaki River; powerhouse at the Otago (south) abutment; first two 15 MW units 1 January 1935; seven units, 105 MW.

contact-clyde.title: Clyde hydro power station
contact-clyde.note: On the Clutha River in Central Otago; Lake Dunstan; commissioned 1992; max capacity 464 MW from four turbine generator units; annual output 2,250 GWh; the largest concrete gravity dam in New Zealand; about one million m³ of concrete in the dam and 200,000 m³ in the powerhouse.

contact-roxburgh.title: Roxburgh hydro power station
contact-roxburgh.note: Clutha River, Central Otago; commissioned 1956 and 1962; max capacity 320 MW; annual output 1,750 GWh; eight generators, the first commissioned in 1956; concrete gravity dam; lake of nearly 6 km².

contact-clutha-scheme.title: Clutha Mata Au Hydro Scheme
contact-clutha-scheme.note: The scheme name. Roxburgh turbine upgrade: four of eight turbines replaced 2024–2026, the first operational January 2025; +44 GWh a year; commissioned 1956–1962 with eight turbines made in Canada by Dominion Turbines.

contact-roxburgh-turbines-2024.title: New turbines at Contact's Roxburgh dam to create more renewable energy (10 June 2024)
contact-roxburgh-turbines-2024.note: Commissioned 1956–1962; eight original Canadian-built turbines, the first four installed 1956–57 and the second four 1960–61; four replaced by Voith, first components on site 7 June 2024; +44 GWh a year; 320 MW.

voith-roxburgh-2025.title: Voith completes second turbine upgrade at New Zealand's Roxburgh hydropower station (30 September 2025)
voith-roxburgh-2025.note: Four of the eight original 40 MW units being replaced; first upgrade finished December 2024; second handed over mid-August 2025.

gazette-1996-174.title: New Zealand Gazette, 2 December 1996, issue 174: ECNZ financial statements
gazette-1996-174.publisher: New Zealand Gazette (Victoria University of Wellington Library archive)
gazette-1996-174.note: Page 4597, note 26: ECNZ agreed with Contact on 13 November 1995 to sell 8 power stations on 1 February 1996: New Plymouth, Stratford, Whirinaki, Otahuhu, Wairakei, Ohaaki, Clyde and Roxburgh, with the Clutha River and geothermal development sites.

teara-hydro-4.title: Hydroelectricity: Hydro and the environment (John E. Martin)
teara-hydro-4.publisher: Te Ara, the Encyclopedia of New Zealand (Manatū Taonga)
teara-hydro-4.note: Clyde: high dam chosen 1976, construction began 1979, empowering legislation 1982, dam finished 1990, commissioned 1992 after extensive stabilisation in the gorge that became Lake Dunstan.

paperspast-press-1988-12-08.title: Clyde power project nears completion (The Press, 8 December 1988, page 36)
paperspast-press-1988-12-08.publisher: Papers Past (National Library of New Zealand)
paperspast-press-1988-12-08.note: The project was being built for the Electricity Corporation; when complete it would produce 432 MW from its four generating turbines.

wp-roxburgh-dam.title: Roxburgh Dam
wp-roxburgh-dam.note: Grade B. On the Clutha River / Mata-Au about 9 km north of Roxburgh; creates Lake Roxburgh; approved by the Labour Government in December 1947; commissioned 1956–1962; 320 MW, 8 turbines.

meridian-west-wind.title: West Wind farm
meridian-west-wind.note: Mākara, west of Wellington; construction 2007, fully operational 2009; 62 turbines, up to 142.6 MW; temporary wharf at Oteranga Bay and 33 km of roads; recreation area.

meridian-te-apiti.title: Te Āpiti Wind Farm
meridian-te-apiti.note: 55 turbines north of the Manawatū Gorge, up to 90.75 MW; Meridian's first wind farm and the first to supply the national grid; construction 2003, fully operational 2004.

meridian-te-uku.title: Te Uku Wind Farm
meridian-te-uku.note: 28 turbines near Raglan, 64.4 MW; construction 2009, "fully operational in 2010"; Wharauroa Plateau; built in alliance with WEL Networks, which built the 25 km 33 kV line.

meridian-mill-creek.title: Mill Creek wind farm
meridian-mill-creek.note: North-west of Wellington near Ōhāriu Valley; fully operational since 2014; 26 turbines, up to 59.8 MW; private farms; 800,000 m3 of earthworks, 19 km of tracks.

meridian-white-hill.title: White Hill Wind Farm
meridian-white-hill.note: Southland, forestry land south-east of Mossburn; 29 turbines, up to 58 MW; Meridian's second wind farm, the first in the South Island; construction 2006, fully operational 2007.

meridian-harapaki.title: Harapaki Wind Farm
meridian-harapaki.note: 41 turbines, 176 MW; Maungaharuru Range, about 35 km north-west of Napier; complete July 2024; three-year build, within the $448m budget.

meridian-te-rere-hau.title: Te Rere Hau Wind (repowering project)
meridian-te-rere-hau.note: Built 2006 with five 500 kW turbines; "currently has 91 turbines with a total installed capacity of 45.5MW"; Meridian completed the acquisition of NZ Windfarms in July 2025; repowering up to 40 turbines and 172 MW, completion 2030.

meridian-nzwf-2025.title: High Court approves acquisition of NZ Windfarms (16 July 2025)
meridian-nzwf-2025.note: Scheme to be implemented on 30 July 2025; Meridian to buy all shares in NZ Windfarms, owner of Te Rere Hau; 50-50 repowering joint venture.

meridian-te-uku-2011.title: Te Uku makes the most of Waikato's wind (press release, 10 February 2011)
meridian-te-uku-2011.note: First turbine live 13 Nov 2010; formally switched on 10 Feb 2011 with 17 of 28 generating; all 28 Siemens 2.3 MW turbines (64.4 MW) by early March; WEL built and operates the line.

mercury-tararua.title: Tararua Wind Farm
mercury-tararua.note: 700 ha; stages 1 and 2: 103 Vestas V47-660 kW, 68 MW, commissioned 1999 and 2004, twin 33 kV lines to Powerco; stage 3: 31 Vestas V90-3MW, 93 MW, 2007, tee off the Bunnythorpe-Linton 220 kV line; acquired from Tilt Aug 2021.

mercury-turitea.title: Turitea Wind Farm
mercury-turitea.note: 60 Vestas V112 turbines; 222 MW; commissioned 2023; 12 km 220 kV line to Linton via two on-site substations.

mercury-waipipi.title: Waipipi Wind Farm
mercury-waipipi.note: About 6 km south-east of Pātea; 31 Siemens Gamesa turbines; "Maximum capacity: 113 MW" (others give 133 MW); construction completed March 2021; 11 km 110 kV line to Waverley.

mercury-mahinerangi.title: Mahinerangi Wind Farm
mercury-mahinerangi.note: Stage 1: 12 turbines, 36 MW, commissioned 2011, west of Dunedin near Lake Mahinerangi; Puke Kapo Hau (stage 2): 40 turbines, 192 MW, construction began November 2026.

mercury-kaiwera-downs.title: Kaiwera Downs Wind Farm
mercury-kaiwera-downs.note: Stage 1: 10 turbines, 43 MW, operational November 2023; stage 2: 36 turbines, 155 MW, generating from April 2026; about 2,000 ha. Has slips (stage 1 "2013", "north-west of Gore").

mercury-kaiwera-downs-factsheet.title: Kaiwera Downs Wind Farm stage 2 fact sheet
mercury-kaiwera-downs-factsheet.note: 15 km south-east of Gore off SH93; stage 2 south-east of stage 1; 36 Vestas V136-4.3MW, hub 88 m, tip 156 m; about 4 km of 220 kV line; thanks Gore District Council and Environment Southland.

mercury-kaiwera-downs-2026.title: Mercury opens $486 million Kaiwera Downs Wind Farm expansion (9 September 2026)
mercury-kaiwera-downs-2026.note: Stage 2 opened 9 Sep 2026: 36 turbines, 155 MW; whole farm 198 MW, 675 GWh a year; South Island's largest wind farm; went ahead on the 2024 Tiwai smelter agreement.

mercury-kaiwaikawe.title: Kaiwaikawe Wind Farm
mercury-kaiwaikawe.note: 12 Vestas V162-6.4 MW, tip 206 m; 12 km north-west of Dargaville, two clusters; via Northpower's Dargaville substation to the grid at Maungatapere; first generation July 2026, final commissioning to early 2027.

tilt-tararua-2020.title: New Zealand's largest wind farm turns 20! (media release, 13 February 2020)
tilt-tararua-2020.note: Stage 1: 48 turbines, commercial operation 24 Dec 1999, when Trustpower took ownership; stage 2 added 55 (103 V47-660 kW in all); 700 ha.

tilt-intro-2016.title: Tilt Renewables introduction booklet (2016)
tilt-intro-2016.note: Established October 2016 by the demerger from Trustpower; owns Tararua (stages 1 and 2, 68 MW; stage 3, 93 MW, 2007) and Mahinerangi stage 1 (36 MW, 2011).

tilt-waipipi-2019.title: Investment Decision for Waipipi Wind Farm (NZX, 28 August 2019)
tilt-waipipi-2019.note: 133 MW, formerly Waverley Wind Farm, named by Ngaa Rauru Kiitahi; 31 Siemens Gamesa 4.3 MW turbines, 130 m rotors; $276m; 455 GWh a year sold to Genesis under a 20-year agreement.

genesis-waipipi-2021.title: Waipipi Wind Farm Update (NZX, 5 March 2021)
genesis-waipipi-2021.note: Tilt reached practical completion of the 133 MW Waipipi Wind Farm; all 31 turbines commissioned.

trustpower-mahinerangi-2006.title: TrustPower Modifies Mahinerangi Windfarm Application (29 September 2006)
trustpower-mahinerangi-2006.note: Withdraws the Dunedin City Council application; revised applications for a 200 MW wind farm on private land to the Clutha District and Otago Regional councils.

wp-tararua-wind-farm.title: Tararua Wind Farm
wp-tararua-wind-farm.note: 134 turbines (103 V47, 31 V90-3MW), 161 MW; stage 3 commissioned September 2007; largest NZ wind farm until Turitea (2023).

wp-te-rere-hau.title: Te Rere Hau Wind Farm
wp-te-rere-hau.note: About 11 km east of Palmerston North; stages 2006, 2009, 2011; 97 Windflow 500 two-bladed turbines, 48.5 MW; NZ Windfarms acquired by Meridian; repowering.

wp-waipipi.title: Waipipi Wind Farm
wp-waipipi.note: Proposed 2007 by Allco; Trustpower 2010; consent 2017; first four turbines 16 Nov 2020; all by early 2021; opened June 2021; 31 x 4.3 MW, 133 MW.

wp-mahinerangi.title: Mahinerangi Wind Farm
wp-mahinerangi.note: North side of Lake Mahinerangi, about 50 km west of Dunedin, 600-730 m; consent 2007; first power 21 Feb 2011, all 12 by end of March; Vestas V90-3MW; feeds the Waipori and Deep Stream schemes' 33 kV lines.

wp-turitea.title: Turitea Wind Farm
wp-turitea.note: Council chose Mighty River Power 2005; board of inquiry approved 60 turbines 2011; northern stage 33 x V112-3.6, southern 27 x V112-3.8; first power 30 Jul 2021; opened May 2023; 12 km 220 kV line to Linton.

wp-kaiwera-downs.title: Kaiwera Downs Wind Farm
wp-kaiwera-downs.note: About 15 km south-east of Gore; consent June 2008 (Trustpower); acquired by Mercury 2021; stage 1 10 x V136 at 4.3 MW, opened Nov 2023; 18 km 33 kV line to Gore; stage 2 36 turbines, 2026.

wp-harapaki.title: Harapaki Wind Farm
wp-harapaki.note: Maungaharuru Range near Titiokura Summit; Meridian bought Hawke's Bay Wind Farm Ltd 2010, Unison's consent 2011; generating from Nov 2023, full capacity July 2024; 41 Siemens Gamesa 4.3 MW.

wp-te-apiti.title: Te Āpiti Wind Farm
wp-te-apiti.note: 55 x Vestas NM72 1.65 MW, 90.75 MW; construction Nov 2003, commissioned Dec 2004; first NZ wind farm connected directly to the grid (Woodville, 4.5 km line); life extended after a 2024 end-of-life study.

wp-west-wind.title: West Wind Wind Farm
wp-west-wind.note: Terawhiti Station and Mākara; construction Sept 2007; opened April 2009 (first 15 turbines); 62 x Siemens SWT-2.3-82 VS, 142.6 MW; hard tees into two Central Park-Wilton circuits.

wp-te-uku.title: Te Uku Wind Farm
wp-te-uku.note: 28 x Siemens SWT-2.3-101; fully operational 10 March 2011; says jointly owned by WEL Networks and Meridian; 33 kV line to Te Kowhai substation.

wp-mill-creek.title: Mill Creek Wind Farm
wp-mill-creek.note: Ohariu Valley; Environment Court limited it to 26 turbines (2011); construction late 2012; first power May 2014, fully operational Oct 2014; Siemens SWT-2.3-82 VS, 59.8 MW; 33 kV to Wilton.

wp-white-hill.title: White Hill Wind Farm
wp-white-hill.note: Six km south-east of Mossburn; construction March 2006, commissioned October 2007; 29 x Vestas V80-2.0MW, 58 MW. Single-source article.

wp-kaiwaikawe.title: Kaiwaikawe Wind Farm
wp-kaiwaikawe.note: About 10 km north-west of Dargaville; Tilt sought consent as Omamari (2021); Genesis offtake 2021; consent March 2022; Mercury proceeded Dec 2024; 12 x Vestas V162-6.4 MW, 77 MW.

bt-kohira.title: BraveTrace NZECS production device info sheet: Kaitaia Kohirā (v1.1, May 2026)
bt-kohira.note: Registrant Lodestone Energy. Commissioned 24 Nov 2023 (first generation November 2023); 23.7 MW AC, 33.3 MWp DC; 61,000 bifacial panels that track the sun; agrivoltaic. The registrant supplies the figures.

bt-lauriston.title: BraveTrace NZECS production device info sheet: Lauriston Solar Farm (v1.0)
bt-lauriston.note: Registrant Genesis Energy. Commissioned 8 Feb 2025 (full generation February 2025); 47 MW AC, 63 MWp DC; 93 ha leased from a farming family, grazed by sheep; around 90,000 panels.

bt-pukenui.title: BraveTrace NZECS production device info sheet: Pukenui Solar Farm (v1.0, December 2025)
bt-pukenui.note: Registrant Project Pukenui LP (certificates sold through Aquila). Commissioned 16 Jun 2025; 17.16 MW AC, 20.8 MWp DC; 35,000 panels; developed with Te Aupōuri.

bt-rangitaiki.title: BraveTrace NZECS production device info sheet: Edgecumbe Rangitaiki (v1.2, May 2026)
bt-rangitaiki.note: Registrant Lodestone Energy. Commissioned 6 Mar 2024; 23.7 MW AC, 32.4 MWp DC; 59,600 tracking bifacial panels; name gifted by Ngāti Awa.

bt-ruawai.title: BraveTrace NZECS production device info sheet: Ruawai Te Puna Mauri ō Omaru (v1.0, December 2025)
bt-ruawai.note: Registrant Northpower. Commissioned 19 Dec 2024; lists AC 19.3 MW and DC 16.8 MWp, which look swapped or out of date after the July 2025 extension: not used for capacity. Bifacial tracking panels.

bt-taiohi.title: BraveTrace NZECS production device info sheet: Taiohi Solar Farm (v1.0, February 2026)
bt-taiohi.note: Registrant NewPower Energy. Commissioned 1 Dec 2025; 22.4 MW AC, 33.1 MWp DC; more than 47,000 panels; the name means youthful.

bt-te-herenga.title: BraveTrace NZECS production device info sheet: Waiotahe Te Herenga o Te Rā (v1.1, May 2026)
bt-te-herenga.note: Registrant Lodestone Energy. First generation December 2024, commissioned 20 Jan 2025; 30 MW AC, 42.9 MWp DC; 71,600 tracking bifacial panels; name gifted by Te Ūpokorehe.

bt-twin-rivers.title: BraveTrace NZECS production device info sheet: Rānui Twin Rivers Solar Farm (v1.0, February 2026)
bt-twin-rivers.note: Registrant Rānui Twin Rivers Asset LP. Commissioned 16 Dec 2025; 24 MW AC, 30 MWp DC; 34 ha between the Victoria and Takahue rivers, near Kaitāia; 55,832 panels; Top Energy's network; developed with Te Paatu; urupā under covenant.

bt-whitianga.title: BraveTrace NZECS production device info sheet: Whitianga Pāmu Rā ki (v1.0)
bt-whitianga.note: Registrant Lodestone Energy. Commissioned 17 Nov 2025; 23.7 MW AC, 33 MWp DC; 53,400 tracking bifacial panels; name gifted by Ngāti Hei.

contact-kowhai-park.title: Kōwhai Park Solar Farm
contact-kowhai-park.note: Operational as of October 2026; maximum 150 MWac; 275 GWh a year; 230 ha; about 300,000 panels; joint venture with Lightsource bp (formed April 2022); Contact's first completed solar farm.

evsandbeyond-clandeboye.title: Lodestone powers up first South Island solar farm (7 Aug 2026)
evsandbeyond-clandeboye.note: First power at Clandeboye, north of Temuka; 27.7 MW; the first grid-scale solar farm on Alpine Energy's network.

harmony-tauhei-close.title: Harmony Energy and First Renewables Joint Venture successfully complete financial close on New Zealand's largest solar farm (Jan 2025)
harmony-tauhei-close.note: 202 MWp on 182 ha near Te Aroha; 280 GWh a year; Meridian buys 100% of output for 10 years; connects to Transpower's 110 kV network at Waihou substation; joint venture of Harmony Energy and First Renewables (Clarus).

lodestone-clandeboye.title: Clandeboye Solar Farm
lodestone-clandeboye.note: Read through search results. A 42 ha former dairy site with about 45,000 single-portrait (1P) bifacial panels and 6 inverters; the landowner runs sheep on it.

lodestone-clandeboye-groundbreaking.title: From Dairy to Solar: Lodestone breaks ground at South Island Clandeboye site (22 Sep 2025)
lodestone-clandeboye-groundbreaking.note: Read through search results. Groundbreaking on 19 Sep 2025 for a 27.7 MWp farm.

lodestone-solar-farms.title: Our solar farms
lodestone-solar-farms.note: Read through search results: the site (now lodestone.co.nz) refuses automated reads. Kohirā: first generation Nov 2023, 56 GWh a year, 61,000+ panels; Rangitaiki: March 2024, 54 GWh, 59,000+; Te Herenga o Te Rā: Dec 2024, 69 GWh, 71,000+; Pāmu Rā ki Whitianga: first power Nov 2025, 49 GWh, 53,400+; Clandeboye: 43 GWh, 45,000+.

meridian-ruakaka-construction.title: Construction on NZ's latest solar farm gets underway (Oct 2025)
meridian-ruakaka-construction.note: Construction under way; 130 MW; 250,000 panels; up to 230 GWh a year; first generation late 2026, full generation early 2027; 35-year life.

meridian-ruakaka-fid.title: Meridian to proceed with $227m Ruakākā Solar Farm (25 Mar 2025)
meridian-ruakaka-fid.note: 130 MW, south of Whangārei; Meridian's first NZ solar farm; 250,000 panels; up to 230 GWh a year; beside the 100 MW Ruakākā battery, completing the Ruakākā Energy Park; first generation late 2026, full generation early 2027.

northpower-ruawai.title: Te Puna Mauri ō Omaru Solar Farm: Bringing power home
northpower-ruawai.note: Ruawai; start March 2024; stage 1 completed December 2024, stage 2 July 2025; about 20 MWdc (stage 1 was 16.8 MWdc); Nextracker among the suppliers; name gifted by Te Uri o Hau; community-owned.

omeheu-site.title: Omeheu Solar Farm (project site)
omeheu-site.note: Owned by Aquila Clean Energy APAC; 30 ha near Edgecumbe (Western Drain Road and Putiki Road); about 63,000 panels on fixed galvanised-steel frames in east-west rows, at most 2.29 m high; seven inverters; switch-on June 2026; connects through the nearby Edgecumbe substation; name gifted by Te Rūnanga o Ngāti Awa in March 2024.

pvtech-lauriston.title: Genesis, FRV Australia open New Zealand's 'largest' solar PV power plant (30 Apr 2025)
pvtech-lauriston.note: 63 MWp; a joint venture of Genesis and FRV Australia; opened 29 April 2025; 93 ha; over 90,000 modules. Mounting not stated.

pvtech-omeheu.title: Aquila Clean Energy energises 38MW solar PV plant in New Zealand's Bay of Plenty (23 Jul 2026)
pvtech-omeheu.note: Omeheu energised (38 MW); Aquila took sole ownership of Omeheu and Pukenui in January 2026 after concluding its joint venture with Far North Solar Farm; Pukenui 20.8 MWp, commissioned October 2025.

pvtech-tauhei.title: Harmony Energy energises New Zealand's largest solar PV plant (16 Jul 2026)
pvtech-tauhei.note: Energised; 202 MWp; joint venture of Harmony Energy New Zealand and Igneo Infrastructure Partners; full commercial operation targeted for Sep–Oct 2026.

scoop-whitianga.title: Lodestone Energy Powers Up Coromandel's First Utility-Scale Solar Farm (4 Dec 2025)
scoop-whitianga.note: Lodestone's release: Pāmu Rā ki Whitianga, on the outskirts of Whitianga, the region's first utility-scale solar farm.

solarquarter-dannevirke.title: GameChange Energy Commissions Tracker System at 23 MWp Dannevirke Solar Farm in New Zealand (25 Aug 2026)
solarquarter-dannevirke.note: Bright Fern Energy's 23 MWp farm; GameChange Genius Tracker 1P (single-axis); designed for seismic conditions, undulating terrain and high wind.

tararua-dc-solar-consents.title: Response to request for copies of resource consents, solar farms, Dannevirke
tararua-dc-solar-consents.note: Read through search results (the PDF would not download). Consent and variations for Dannevirke Solar Farm Ltd, 440 Tamaki River Road, Dannevirke (2024–2025).

teao-papareireia.title: Retirement villages to be powered by Ngāpuhi's new Northland solar farm (11 Nov 2024)
teao-papareireia.note: Construction begun on a 21 MW array near Maungatūroto; up to 32 GWh a year; sole customer Ryman Healthcare (10-year agreement); joint venture of Tupu Tonu, Purpose Capital and Harbour Infrastructure; the name's meaning.

wd-q132019984.title: Wikidata item Q132019984
wd-q132019984.note: Te Puna Mauri ō Omaru: coordinates at Ruawai.

wel-taiohi-energised.title: NewPower energises Taiohi Solar Farm, delivering new resilience for the Waikato region
wel-taiohi-energised.note: 33 MW farm at Rangiriri; more than 47,000 panels; developer and owner NewPower Energy (WEL Networks group); the name, meaning youthful, gifted by mana whenua; Maurea Marae.

wel-taiohi-opened.title: Taiohi Solar Farm strengthens Waikato's energy resilience (Apr 2026)
wel-taiohi-opened.note: Officially opened; 32 ha; more than 47,000 panels; about 44.6 GWh a year; partnership with Maurea Marae.

wp-papareireia.title: Papareireiā Solar Farm
wp-papareireia.note: Coordinates; 21 MWp DC; also known as the Ryman Healthcare Solar Farm; officially commissioned December 2025 (citing Scoop).

genesis-huntly.title: Huntly Power Station
genesis-huntly.note: By capacity the country's largest station (1,200 MW). Rankine units: three 250 MW (gas/coal), commissioned between 1982 and 1985, used for baseload, hydro-firming and peaking. Unit 5 (previously e3p, Energy Efficiency Enhancement Project): 403 MW combined cycle on natural gas, commissioned June 2007 (250 MW gas turbine, heat-recovery steam generator, 135 MW steam turbine). Unit 6: 50.8 MW open cycle gas turbine, commissioned 2004, gas or diesel, run as a peaking unit.

genesis-nzx-2025-08.title: Agreements signed for Huntly capacity (market release, 4 August 2025)
genesis-nzx-2025-08.note: Three Rankine units, each 240 MW (720 MW in total), able to run on gas and coal; one Rankine unit was due to be decommissioned in February 2026.

comcom-490.title: Decision 490: Genesis Power Limited and Natural Gas Corporation Holdings Limited (4 February 2003)
comcom-490.note: Genesis's generation in 2003: Huntly (gas and coal) 1,000 MW, Te Awamutu cogeneration 54 MW, Kinleith cogeneration 40 MW, and its hydro and wind.

comcom-491.title: Decision 491: Contact Energy Limited and Natural Gas Corporation Holdings Limited (4 February 2003)
comcom-491.note: TCC completed 1998, 3 km east of Stratford, 354 MW (+10 MW supplementary firing), owned by NGC's Stratford Power Ltd. Contact's portfolio: Otahuhu A (diesel) 40, Otahuhu B 380, Te Rapa cogeneration 44, New Plymouth 400 MW. NGC had owned 50% of Southdown and sold it to its joint venture partner Mighty River Power; NGC and Todd Energy each own 50% of the Kapuni Energy joint venture, which generates electricity and steam at the Kapuni gas treatment plant site.

contact-whirinaki.title: Whirinaki Peaker Plant
contact-whirinaki.note: Whirinaki, Hawke's Bay; commissioned 2004; max capacity 156 MW (the text says 155 MW); three fast-start units, cold start to generating in 20 to 30 minutes; about four million litres of diesel on site, 92 hours at full capacity.

contact-tcc-2022.title: TCC power station returns to limited service (4 April 2022)
contact-tcc-2022.note: Contact commissioned the Stratford Peakers next to TCC in 2011: two fast-start gas turbine peaking units, cold start to full load in 10 minutes, up to 200 MW. (It says TCC was commissioned in 1996; other sources give 1998.)

contact-cdc-2026.title: Contact partners with CDC to explore data centre development (market release, 10 August 2026)
contact-cdc-2026.note: TCC retired earlier in 2026, having reached end of life; Contact's existing 200 MW of generation at Stratford is not affected.

todd-power-plants.title: Power plants
todd-power-plants.note: Todd Energy operates the Junction Road and McKee power plants in north Taranaki, used by Nova Energy at times of high demand or when other generation is unavailable. Junction Road: 100 MW, commissioned 2020, full output in 15 minutes, near Junction Road (State Highway 3). McKee: 100 MW, in use since 2012, full output in 15 minutes, at the McKee Production Station on Tariki Road east of Inglewood.

todd-jrpp-2018.title: Junction Road power plant (news release, 9 July 2018)
todd-jrpp-2018.note: Todd Generation confirms plans to build a gas-fired peaking plant about 7 km south of New Plymouth, supplied with gas from the First Gas pipeline and connected to the national grid.

todd-kapuni.title: Kapuni
todd-kapuni.note: Kapuni field history; Todd's Kapuni Gas Treatment Plant; mid-1990s gas supply contracts to the 70 MW Fonterra/Todd Energy co-generation plant at Whareroa near Hāwera (1996); the field's gathering system feeds the pipeline to the co-generation plant at Whareroa.

trc-jrpp-2024.title: Nova Energy Ltd Junction Road Power Plant monitoring programme annual report 2023/24 (Technical Report 2024-59)
trc-jrpp-2024.note: Nova Energy operates the plant at 688 Junction Road, New Plymouth: two 50 MW open cycle aero-derivative gas turbines on natural gas; commissioning March 2020, commercial operation from 15 May 2020; formerly operated by Todd Generation, whose consents moved to Nova on 1 June 2022.

trc-kgtp-2022.title: Todd Petroleum Mining Company Ltd Kapuni Gas Treatment Plant monitoring programme annual report (Technical Report 22-79)
trc-kgtp-2022.note: The Kapuni Gas Treatment Plant is on Palmer Road, Kapuni, in the Kapuni catchment, South Taranaki; operated by Todd Petroleum Mining Company.

ea-whareroa-2026.title: Whareroa Cogeneration Plant: notice of transfer of ownership and application for type B industrial co-generator classification (3 July 2026)
ea-whareroa-2026.note: From 1 August 2026 Whareroa Cogeneration Limited, a Fonterra subsidiary, owns and runs the plant, Fonterra buying Nova Energy's remaining 50% of the Whareroa Cogeneration Joint Venture. Embedded at HWA1101 and HWA1102. Four 10 MW gas turbines with heat recovery boilers, steam to a 28 MW steam turbine or the factory; steam is its main purpose. Fonterra is adding two 34 MW electric boilers; the site needs about 95 MW of process heat.

ea-cogen-register.title: Register of generators approved as industrial co-generators (updated 17 August 2022)
ea-cogen-register.note: Carter Holt Harvey Pulp and Paper: Kinleith Mill turbine generator (type B, 2015). Todd Energy and Whareroa Power unincorporated joint venture: all 5 units at the Whareroa co-generator (type B, 2019). Norske Skog Tasman: 4 units at Kawerau (type A, 2013). Kapuni Energy Joint Venture: all 4 generation units (type A, 2020). Alinta ENZ: kilns cogen plant, Glenbrook Power Station (type B, 2020).

vector-kapuni-2019.title: Vector to sell Kapuni assets and enter into new long term natural gas and LPG supply arrangements (3 December 2019)
vector-kapuni-2019.note: Vector to transfer the Kapuni Gas Treatment Plant and related assets, and its 50% of the Kapuni Energy Joint Venture, to Todd Petroleum Mining Company. The plant processes all the gas from the Kapuni field.

fonterra-electrification-2025.title: Fonterra announces electrification plans to future-proof operations (29 January 2025)
fonterra-electrification-2025.note: Electrode boilers at Whareroa (two, first stage, $64 million) and Edgecumbe ($57 million; the site moves from steam and electricity from its co-generation plant to an electrode boiler).

nzherald-chh-kinleith.title: Carter Holt Harvey weighs in for court bout
nzherald-chh-kinleith.note: Carter Holt Harvey's High Court claim against Genesis Power and Rolls-Royce over the Kinleith co-generation plant, installed in 1997, which burns wood waste to make steam and electricity. Date not shown in the search copy (early 2000s).

wp-huntly.title: Huntly Power Station
wp-huntly.note: Grade B. Units 1–4 (250 MW, coal or gas), unit 6 (2004), unit 5 CCGT (2007, 250 + 153 MW); one unit stored Dec 2012, a second retired Jun 2015; gas for units 5 and 6 from Taranaki; Waikato River cooling.

wp-stratford.title: Stratford Power Station
wp-stratford.note: Grade B. Original 200 MW gas turbine plant (four 50 MW FT4 twin-paks) completed June 1976, removed 2001; TCC 377 MW, built 1996–98, bought by Contact 2003, Pātea River cooling; two LMS100 peakers (200 MW) built 2009–10, opened 31 May 2011.

wp-new-plymouth.title: New Plymouth Power Station
wp-new-plymouth.note: Grade B. 600 MW at Port Taranaki, gas or fuel oil, 1974–2008; five 120 MW units (first Feb 1974, fifth 1976); NZED, NZE, ECNZ, Contact; asbestos found 2007; unit 3 back May–Dec 2008; site sold to Port Taranaki and Methanex 2013; demolished 2014–15.

wp-otahuhu.title: Ōtāhuhu Power Station
wp-otahuhu.note: Grade B. A: four 45 MW gas turbines (1968), two Olympus twin-paks (1978), out of generation in the late 1990s, then reactive power until decommissioned Nov 2013. B: combined cycle, Siemens V94.3A single shaft, Jan 2000, 385 MW then ~404 MW (2005), ceased end Sep 2015. Site sold 2016.

wp-southdown.title: Southdown, New Zealand (Southdown Co-generation Facility section)
wp-southdown.note: Grade B. Gas combined cycle cogeneration; developed by a TransAlta and Mercury Energy joint venture; commissioned Dec 1996 with two LM6000s and a steam turbine; third LM6000 2007; 170 MW after upgrades; steam to nearby industry; Mighty River Power bought 50% in 2000 and the rest in 2002; closure announced Mar 2015; demolished 2022–24.

wp-whirinaki.title: Whirinaki Power Station
wp-whirinaki.note: Grade B. NZED gas turbine station (1978, 220 MW, four FT4 twin-paks, diesel): one unit moved to the Te Awamutu dairy factory cogeneration plant in 1993, three sold to Australia 2001. Reserve plant built for the government, opened June 2004 ($150 million), three FT8 twin-paks, 155 MW, run by Contact; Contact bought it 22 Dec 2011.

wp-te-rapa.title: Te Rapa cogeneration
wp-te-rapa.note: Grade B. 44 MW at Fonterra's Te Rapa dairy factory, Contact Energy, commissioned 1999; GE Frame 6B with HRSG; planned 150 MW cut to 45 MW (1997); Contact announced 21 Jun 2022 it would close by June 2023 when the Fonterra supply contract ended.

wp-glenbrook.title: Glenbrook Power Station
wp-glenbrook.note: Grade B. 112 MW cogeneration integrated into the New Zealand Steel plant at Glenbrook; surplus gas from the iron-making kilns; two plants, 1987 and 1997.

wp-mckee.title: McKee power station
wp-mckee.note: Grade B. Gas-fired plant at the McKee production station, north Taranaki; owned and operated by Nova Energy; 100 MW open cycle, two GE LM6000s, officially opened March 2013.

wp-kinleith-mill.title: Kinleith Mill
wp-kinleith-mill.note: Grade B. Pulp and paper mill at Kinleith, Tokoroa, operated by Oji Fibre Solutions (formerly Carter Holt Harvey); its cogeneration plant burns wood waste (about 35 MW used on site); paper production ceased June 2025, pulp continues.

wd-q2944688.title: Wikidata item Q2944688
wd-q2944688.note: New Plymouth Power Station: coordinates; 600 MW.

wd-q7108372.title: Wikidata item Q7108372
wd-q7108372.note: Otahuhu Power Station (the site): coordinates; 404 MW; service entry 1968.

wd-q12002141.title: Wikidata item Q12002141
wd-q12002141.note: Southdown Power Station: coordinates; 170 MW; service entry Dec 1996.

wd-q7690951.title: Wikidata item Q7690951
wd-q7690951.note: Te Rapa cogeneration: coordinates; 44 MW; inception 1999.

contact-geothermal.title: Geothermal sites
contact-geothermal.note: Contact's six geothermal station pages (Ōhaaki, Poihipi Road, Te Mihi, Wairākei, Te Huka, Tauhara); names Te Huka 3 among its new stations.

contact-wairakei.title: Wairākei geothermal power station
contact-wairakei.note: Location Wairākei, Taupō; commissioned November 1958; max capacity 133 MW (the page's figure); annual output 1,062 GWh; A and B stations with 10 steam turbines of 4–30 MW (older text: the Nov 2024 announcement lists 8 units).

contact-te-mihi.title: Te Mihi geothermal power station
contact-te-mihi.note: Wairākei, Taupō; commissioned 2014; max capacity 166 MW; annual output 1,384 GWh; on the Wairakei geothermal field, northwest of Taupō.

contact-poihipi.title: Poihipi Road geothermal power station
contact-poihipi.note: Wairākei, Taupō; commissioned 1997; bought by Contact in 2000; on the Wairākei geothermal system, operated as part of the Wairakei steamfield; capacity 51 MW; annual output 309 GWh.

contact-ohaaki.title: Ohaaki geothermal power station
contact-ohaaki.note: Waikato, Taupō; commissioned 1989; max capacity 43.7 MW; annual output 315 GWh; production wells average 1.2 km deep, up to 280°C; 105 m natural-convection cooling tower.

contact-te-huka.title: Te Huka geothermal power station
contact-te-huka.note: Wairākei, Taupō; commissioned 2010; about 82 MW (the page's figure, which appears to include Te Huka 3); binary (organic Rankine cycle); the first power station on the Tauhara geothermal steamfield.

contact-tauhara.title: Tauhara geothermal power station
contact-tauhara.note: Taupō; commissioned 2024; max capacity 174 MW; annual output 1,260 GWh; opened November 2024 (officially 22 November); the world's largest single-shaft geothermal turbine, 3,000 rpm; 220 m cooling tower; triple-flash separation plant; 14 km of pipelines to the wells.

contact-tauhara-opening-2024.title: New Zealand's energy security boosted as Contact opens new geothermal power station (22 November 2024)
contact-tauhara-opening-2024.note: Tauhara officially opened 22 Nov 2024 by the Prime Minister; 174 MW at full capacity; $924 million; first supplied the grid 6 May 2024; three and a half years to build; Te Huka 3 in final commissioning.

contact-wairakei-2024.title: Contact invests to redevelop Wairakei (NZX/ASX announcement and presentation, 13 November 2024)
contact-wairakei-2024.note: Te Mihi Stage 2 (101 MW, two Ormat binary units) to be online by Q3 2027; Wairakei planned to close June 2026, now all units to mid-2027, then two B units and one binary unit (67 MW installed) to June 2031 when its resource consent ends. Units today: Wairakei A 3 x 11 MW, Wairakei B 3 x 30 MW, binary 2 x 7 MW.

contact-microsoft-2023.title: Contact signs 10-year renewable energy agreement with Microsoft on new geothermal power station at Te Huka (25 May 2023)
contact-microsoft-2023.note: Te Huka Unit 3: a new 51.4 MW geothermal power station at Te Huka.

thinkgeo-te-huka-3-2024.title: Te Huka 3 geothermal power station in New Zealand starts grid supply (15 October 2024)
thinkgeo-te-huka-3-2024.note: From Contact's announcement: Te Huka Unit 3 supplying the grid for the first time; 15 MW during three weeks of testing, rising to its full 51.4 MW; NZ$300 million; binary cycle using pentane; emissions reinjected; expected fully online by the end of 2024.

nzga-wairakei.title: Wairakei Geothermal System
nzga-wairakei.note: First turbine generated on 15 November 1958; stages 1 and 1A 1956–60, stage 2 (3 x 30 MW) Oct 1963; operator NZ Electricity Department, then ECNZ from 1987, Contact from 1995 (sic). Poihipi built by the Geotherm Joint Venture (1996, 1 x 50 MW Fuji), insolvent for lack of steam, sold to Contact in 2000, linked to the Wairakei steamfield 2006. Wairakei binary (Ormat, 14.3 MW) June 2005. Te Mihi: two 84 MW Toshiba dual-flash turbines, 2014. The Waikato River is the administrative boundary between the Wairakei and Tauhara fields.

nzga-tauhara.title: Tauhara Geothermal System
nzga-tauhara.note: Te Huka binary plant (24 MWe) commissioned 2010, its two units upgraded to 26 MWe in 2012; Tauhara (Fuji 174 MWe triple-flash condensing turbine, Tauhara East sector) and Te Huka unit 3 (50 MWe Ormat binary, Tauhara Central sector) under construction (page written before 2024). The Crown sold most of its Tauhara wells and rights to Contact in the late 1990s.

nzga-ohaaki.title: Ohaaki Geothermal System
nzga-ohaaki.note: The Ohaaki-Broadlands geothermal system, 20 km northeast of Taupō. Station commissioned 1989 (owner Contact) with 114 MWe; declining steam led to deratings, including decommissioning one high-pressure turbine; output fell to about 30 MWe, restored to about 50 MWe by new wells.

enz-ohaaki.title: Ōhaaki Power Station (heritage record)
enz-ohaaki.note: On the Broadlands geothermal field about 25 km north of Wairakei; opened 1989, adding 108 MW; five separation plants; separated water reinjected at 150°C; natural-draught cooling tower, a first for New Zealand. Designer Works Corp, Design Power, Rankine and Hill; built by Works Corporation, Power Build, Wilkins and Davies.

enz-wairakei.title: Wairākei Geothermal Power Development (heritage record)
enz-wairakei.note: The world's second geothermal power station and the first to use flash steam from geothermal water; commissioned 1958, completed 1963; beside the Waikato River 10 km north of Taupō.

teara-geothermal-2.title: Geothermal energy: Wairākei geothermal power station (Carol Stewart, 2 March 2009)
teara-geothermal-2.publisher: Te Ara, the Encyclopedia of New Zealand (Manatū Taonga)
teara-geothermal-2.note: Exploratory drilling from 1949; at first a joint venture with the UK Atomic Energy Authority to produce power and heavy water, approved 1954, the UKAEA withdrew in 1956; built 1958–63; the world's second geothermal power station and the first to use wet steam.

teara-ohaki-photo.title: Ōhākī power station (photograph caption)
teara-ohaki-photo.publisher: Te Ara, the Encyclopedia of New Zealand (Manatū Taonga)
teara-ohaki-photo.note: Officially opened 31 October 1989; New Zealand's second geothermal power station and the first to inject waste geothermal fluid back into the ground.

tutangata-1986-04.title: Ohaaki will be a spectacular sight (Tu Tangata, issue 29, 1 April 1986, page 40)
tutangata-1986-04.note: Final Government approval to build came in 1982; on Ngāti Tahu land leased on the west bank of the Waikato River; commercial operation planned from October 1988; two intermediate-pressure and two high-pressure turbo-generators, the high-pressure sets refurbished from Wairakei.

wp-wairakei.title: Wairakei Power Station
wp-wairakei.note: Commissioned November 1958; owner Contact Energy; binary plant 2005; unit list (A: six 11.2 MW; B: three 30 MW; unit 14, 4 MW; binary 14 MW).

wp-te-mihi.title: Te Mihi Power Station
wp-te-mihi.note: Construction began March 2011; commissioned May 2014; officially opened August 2014; two 83 MW Toshiba steam turbines; $623 million.

wp-poihipi.title: Poihipi Power Station
wp-poihipi.note: 55 MW; commissioned 1996 (infobox); a 55 MW Fuji Electric set built for The Geysers in California but never run, converted to 50 Hz (section unsourced).

wp-ohaaki.title: Ohaaki Power Station
wp-ohaaki.note: Built for 104 MW, commissioned 1989; three turbines now in operation; 105 m natural-draft cooling tower, the only one in New Zealand; beside Ohaaki Marae (Ngāti Tahu).

wp-te-huka.title: Te Huka Power Station
wp-te-huka.note: Also known as Tauhara One, formerly Centennial Drive binary; Ormat binary plant on the Tauhara steamfield; opened May 2010; 33 kV line to Transpower's Wairakei substation.

wp-tauhara.title: Tauhara Power Station
wp-tauhara.note: Previously known as Tauhara 2; developed by Contact Energy and the Tauhara Moana Trust; construction began 31 March 2021; opened November 2024; 174 MW.

mercury-geothermal.title: Geothermal generation
mercury-geothermal.note: Mercury's five geothermal stations: Kawerau, Mōkai (owned with Tuaropaki Power Company), Ngā Awa Pūrua and Rotokawa (with Tauhara North No.2 Trust) and Ngā Tamariki; Kawerau, Ngā Awa Pūrua and Ngā Tamariki completed 2008–13.

mercury-kawerau.title: Kawerau Geothermal Station
mercury-kawerau.note: Opened 2008; total installed capacity 107 MW; 875 GWh a year; a Fuji Electric–Sumitomo single-shaft, dual-flash plant; new wells drilled since it opened; steam also serves Kawerau's industrial hub.

mercury-mokai.title: Mōkai Geothermal Power Station
mercury-mokai.note: On the Mōkai field, 30 km northwest of Taupō; opened 2000; 113 MW; 930 GWh a year; owned by Tūaropaki Trust (75%) and Mercury (25%); combined cycle with 10 binary turbines and two steam turbines; 55 MW in 2000, +38 MW in 2005, +20 MW in 2008.

mercury-nga-awa-purua.title: Ngā Awa Pūrua Geothermal Power Station
mercury-nga-awa-purua.note: Opened 2010; 139 MW installed; 755 GWh a year (the page's figure); on the Rotokawa geothermal field, 14 km northeast of Taupō; owned by Tauhara North No.2 Trust (35%) and Mercury (65%); a Fuji Electric–Sumitomo triple-flash plant; wells average 2,500 m; 10-fan cooling tower.

mercury-nga-tamariki.title: Ngā Tamariki Geothermal Station
mercury-nga-tamariki.note: 17 km northeast of Taupō; opened 2013 with four binary units; fifth unit: construction from May 2024, first power to the grid January 2026, opened March 2026; 86 MW to 132 MW installed, about 1,120 GWh a year; resource consents held jointly with Tauhara North No.2 Trust; on Wairakei Pastoral Estate; reinjects non-condensable gases.

mercury-rotokawa.title: Rotokawa Geothermal Station
mercury-rotokawa.note: Opened 1997; 34 MW installed; 286 GWh a year; on the Rotokawa field, 14 km northeast of Taupō; combined cycle; owned by Mercury, with Tauhara North No.2 Trust holding 35% of the steamfield; 25 MW when commissioned, a 6 MW turbine added in 2003 and 3 MW since.

nzga-kawerau.title: Kawerau Geothermal Field
nzga-kawerau.note: In the Bay of Plenty Region, in both Kawerau and Whakatāne districts; supplying steam to mills since 1957; consent holders Mercury, Ngāti Tūwharetoa Geothermal Assets, Geothermal Developments and the Te Ahi O Māui Partnership; production wells 950–2,100 m.

nzga-rotokawa.title: Rotokawa Geothermal System
nzga-rotokawa.note: Between Tauhara and Ohaaki, about 10 km northeast of Taupō; Rotokawa (Ormat combined cycle, 24 MWe) commissioned 1997, expanded to 34 MWe in 2003; steamfield owned by the Rotokawa Joint Venture (Tauhara North No.2 Trust and Mercury, 50:50), plant by Rotokawa Generation (Mercury); Ngā Awa Pūrua 138 MWe triple flash, 2010. Plant table: Rotokawa 1997, 4 units (1 flash, 3 binary); extension 2003, 1 binary unit; Ngā Awa Pūrua 2010, 1 triple-flash unit.

nzga-ngatamariki.title: Ngā Tamariki Geothermal System
nzga-ngatamariki.note: 17 km northeast of Taupō; Crown exploration wells 1985–86, Mighty River Power from 2008; station commissioned 2013 with four Ormat 20.5 MWe binary units (82 MWe), owned and operated by Mercury, steamfield and consents jointly with Tauhara North No.2 Trust.

nzga-mokai.title: Mokai Geothermal System
nzga-mokai.note: 20 km north of Taupō; Mokai 1 (1999, 6 units, 55 MWe), Mokai 2 (2005, 5 units, 39 MWe), Mokai 1A (2007, 1 binary unit, 17 MWe); 100% reinjection; also a glasshouse and the Miraka dairy factory; Tuaropaki Power Company.

nzga-generation-2023.title: Geothermal electricity generation activities report 2023
nzga-generation-2023.note: Table 3.1, history of geothermal capacity with owners: Kawerau binary TG1 (1989, 2.4 MW) and TG2 (1993, 3.5 MW), Nova Energy and NTGAL, retired 2014 and 2017; Ngāwhā 1998 (10 MW), OEC3 2008 (15 MW), OEC4 2021 (31 MW); Mokai A 1999; Rotokawa A 1997; Kawerau KGL 2008 (100 MW, rerated +7 MW 2017); TOPP1 2013; TAOM 2018 (25 MW).

ngawhagen-who-we-are.title: Ngāwhā Generation: who we are
ngawhagen-who-we-are.note: The new station (OEC4) generates 32 MW, more than the 25 MW of the two existing stations combined; OEC5, a further 32 MW, is consented.

ngawhagen-opening-2021.title: Ngāwhā Geothermal Power Station official opening (9 July 2021)
ngawhagen-opening-2021.note: OEC4 (32 MW, $189 million) officially opened 9 Jul 2021 with Parahirahi Ngāwhā Waiariki Trust and Ngāti Rangi; first power exported on New Year's Eve after three months of commissioning; three production and three injection wells, 1,350–1,750 m; station capacity now 57 MW.

powermag-kawerau-2009.title: New Zealand Geothermal Station Opens (1 January 2009)
powermag-kawerau-2009.note: Kawerau officially opened in late November 2008; 100 MW; construction began January 2007, operational in August 2008; six production wells 1,900–2,100 m; one steam turbine; grid connection at a substation near the Norske Skog Tasman mill.

wp-kawerau.title: Kawerau Power Station
wp-kawerau.note: The Kawerau field's plants: TG1 (Ormat binary, decommissioned 2014), TG2 (1993, 3.5 MW, removed by 2020), KGL (2008, 100 MW, single Fuji turbine), GDL and others; completed July 2008 by Mighty River Power for NZ$300 million.

wp-mokai.title: Mokai Power Station
wp-mokai.note: Owned by Tuaropaki Power Company (75% Tuaropaki Trust, 25% Mighty River Power) and operated by Mercury; Ormat binary cycle; 55 MW from 1999, +40 MW 2005, 110 MW 2007.

wp-nga-awa-purua.title: Nga Awa Purua Power Station
wp-nga-awa-purua.note: Also known as Rotokawa II; construction began May 2008; first generated 18 January 2010; officially opened 15 May 2010; one 140 MW turbine.

wp-ngatamariki.title: Ngatamariki Power Station
wp-ngatamariki.note: Work began July 2011; operational September 2013; Ormat binary plant; a 220 kV line to Ngā Awa Pūrua, where both stations connect to the grid.

wp-rotokawa.title: Rotokawa Power Station
wp-rotokawa.note: Owned and operated by Mercury; about 10 km northeast of Taupō; Ormat binary cycle.

wp-top-energy.title: Top Energy (Ngāwhā Geothermal Power Station)
wp-top-energy.note: Top Energy owns and operates the Ngāwhā station on the Ngāwhā field; Ormat binary; commissioned 1998, 2008, 2020; coordinates 35°25′03″S 173°51′07″E.

contact-cobb.title: Cobb River hydro power station
contact-cobb.note: Takaka and Cobb Rivers, Tasman; commissioned 1944; max capacity 33 MW; 190 GWh a year; stored water almost 600 m above the station, the greatest head of any NZ power station (the text says this lets 36 MW be generated).

contact-coleridge.title: Coleridge hydro power station
contact-coleridge.note: Rakaia River catchment, Canterbury; commissioned 1914; max 43 MW; 272 GWh; feasibility studies from 1906, construction under way by 1911: the Government's first major hydro project.

contact-highbank.title: Highbank hydro power station
contact-highbank.note: Rakaia River catchment, Canterbury; Highbank 1939–1945, Montalto 1982; max 27 MW; 105 GWh; out of commission while the 27 MW 1945 unit is replaced by a new 19 MW GE unit; six pumps run as 1 MW turbines meanwhile; irrigation has priority in summer.

contact-matahina.title: Matahina hydro power station
contact-matahina.note: Rangitāiki River; commissioned 1967; max 77 MW; 284 GWh; 86 m earth dam, the largest of its kind in the North Island; two generators (low and high flows); Wheao & Flaxy furthest upstream, then Aniwhenua, then Matahina.

contact-mangahao.title: Mangahao hydro power station
contact-mangahao.note: Mangahao and Tokomaru Rivers, Manawatū-Whanganui; commissioned 1924; max 39.9 MW; 131 GWh; several dams.

contact-kaimai.title: Kaimai hydro power scheme
contact-kaimai.note: Kaimai Range, Bay of Plenty; commissioned 1972–1994; max 42 MW; 166 GWh; run of river; four power stations on small daily storage lakes linked by canals and tunnels; Lake McLaren dam releases up to 26 days a year for kayakers.

contact-wheao-flaxy.title: Wheao and Flaxy hydro power stations
contact-wheao-flaxy.note: Rangitāiki River, Bay of Plenty; commissioned 1982; max 26 MW; 111 GWh; Kaingaroa Forest; Rangitāiki River, Wheao River and Flaxy Stream; three dams and two canals; Rangitāiki canal fishery.

contact-patea.title: Pātea hydro power station
contact-patea.note: Pātea River, Taranaki; commissioned 1984; max 32 MW; 108 GWh; 82 m earth-fill dam, the fourth highest in NZ; Lake Rotorangi, 46 km, NZ's longest man-made lake; eel bypass and trap and transfer.

contact-waipori.title: Waipori hydro power scheme
contact-waipori.note: Waipori River, Otago; commissioned 1907–1963; max 93 MW; 189 GWh; four power stations (Waipori 1A, 2A, 3 and 4) in a steep gorge; first built to power Dunedin; Lake Mahinerangi.

contact-deep-stream.title: Deep Stream hydro power station
contact-deep-stream.note: Otago; commissioned 2008; max 6 MW; 20 GWh; sits above the Waipori scheme; water from an existing Deep Stream diversion to a storage reservoir, released to Lake Mahinerangi.

contact-branch-river.title: Branch River hydro power scheme
contact-branch-river.note: Branch River, Marlborough; commissioned 1983; max 11 MW; 56 GWh; run of river, two stations (Wairau and Argyle); 2022 intake upgrade; Lake Argyle and the Branch and Leatham rivers popular with anglers.

contact-dillmans.title: Dillmans (Kumara scheme) hydro power stations
contact-dillmans.note: Kawhaka Creek, West Coast; commissioned 1928; max 11 MW; 47 GWh; Duffers, Dillmans and Kumara stations; Big Wainihinihi, Arahura Wainihinihi and Kawhaka Creek intakes feed Duffers; Loopline and Kapitea reservoirs supply Kumara.

contact-paerau-patearoa.title: Paerau and Patearoa hydro power stations
contact-paerau-patearoa.note: Taieri River, Otago; commissioned 1984; max 12 MW; 61 GWh; run of river in winter; in summer Paerau uses irrigation water stored in Loganburn Reservoir; Patearoa runs only on excess water.

contact-manawa-2025.title: Contact buys Manawa Energy
contact-manawa-2025.note: Contact's acquisition of Manawa Energy completed on Friday 11 July 2025.

nzx-announcements-391276.title: Update on retail sale and Manawa Energy launch (NZX, 2 May 2022)
nzx-announcements-391276.note: Trustpower's name change to Manawa Energy Limited took effect on 2 May 2022, after the sale of its retail business to Mercury.

kce-our-story.title: Our story
kce-our-story.note: Mangahao opened 1924; in 1997 KCE and Todd Mangahao formed a joint venture (KCE Mangahao) to buy Mangahao from the government; KCE sole owner from 2012; Trustpower majority shareholder from 2015; Manawa 2022; Contact the 75% shareholder from 2025.

pioneer-history.title: Our history
pioneer-history.note: Otago Central Electric Power Board 1924; amalgamated with the Teviot Power Board 1960; Central Electric 1993; Pioneer Generation 1999 (kept the generation); Southern Generation LP 2015; Pulse Energy Alliance 2016; renamed Pioneer Energy 2016; acquired 100% of Southern Generation LP 2024.

pioneer-aniwhenua.title: Aniwhenua Hydro
pioneer-aniwhenua.note: Middle of three schemes on the Rangitāiki; built and commissioned by Bay of Plenty Electricity in 1981 (the summary says built 1982, opened by Sir Robert Muldoon); acquired by the Todd Corporation and Nova Energy in 1998; 2.2 km canal; 10 m barrage; two penstocks; 127 GWh; monitored from Alexandra.

pioneer-roaring-meg.title: Roaring Meg Scheme
pioneer-roaring-meg.note: Lower Roaring Meg opened 19 March 1936 (304 m head, 21.8 GWh), financed by two gold-dredging companies and the Otago Central Electric Power Board; Upper Roaring Meg producing from July 1947 (119 m, 6.1 GWh); pipeline upgrade 2023.

pioneer-teviot.title: Teviot Scheme
pioneer-teviot.note: Lake Onslow storage (1981 arch dam over the 1890s one); Marslin dam 1981; stations George 1924 (1,000 kW since 2002), Bridge 1972, Ellis 1981 (ex-Waipori Falls plant), Michelle 1982 (1.6 MW), Horseshoe Bend 1999 (4.3 MW), Kowhai 2010; rejoins the Clutha near Roxburgh.

wp-cobb.title: Cobb Power Station
wp-cobb.note: Hume Pipe Company licence 1935; government took over 1940; first power June 1944; storage dam 1954; isolated supply to Nelson and Tasman until 1955; sold to TransAlta 1999, NGC a year later, TrustPower 2003; six Pelton turbines.

wp-coleridge.title: Coleridge Power Station
wp-coleridge.note: Built from 1911, three units in 1914, nine by 1930; ECNZ (Electricorp) 1987; bought by Trustpower (with Alpine Energy, which withdrew) in 1998 for $90.6 million; five turbines in use after a refurbishment completed in 2008.

wp-highbank.title: Highbank Power Station
wp-highbank.note: Built by the Public Works Department with the Rangitata Diversion Race; opened 16 June 1945; a single unit, then NZ's largest; pumping since 2010; unit replacement Nov 2024 to May 2026 (a new 29 MW turbine and generator).

wp-matahina.title: Matahina Power Station
wp-matahina.note: Ministry of Works; generators commissioned 25 January and April 1967; Electricorp sold it to TrustPower (the article says 1999) for $115 million; Waiohau fault beneath the dam.

wp-mangahao.title: Mangahao Power Station
wp-mangahao.note: Opened 3 November 1924 by William Massey; eight tunnellers died; lines to Wellington, Palmerston North, Hawke's Bay; still says jointly owned by Todd Energy and King Country Energy.

wp-roaring-meg.title: Roaring Meg hydro scheme
wp-roaring-meg.note: Two stations in the Kawarau Gorge near Cromwell; built by the Otago Central Power Board from 1934, commissioned 1936; lower 3.0 MW and upper 1.263 MW, two turbines each.

wp-patea-dam.title: Pātea Dam
wp-patea-dam.note: Built 1980–84; 82 m, fourth highest in NZ; first dam of tertiary sandstone and siltstone fill; Lake Rotorangi 46 km; scheme commissioned May 1984 for the Egmont Electric Power Board; Trustpower/Manawa since 1999; three 10.5 MW sets and a 700 kW auxiliary.

wp-manawa-energy.title: Manawa Energy
wp-manawa-energy.note: Trustpower's history: Tauranga Joint Generation Committee (1965; Lloyd Mandeno 1972, Lower Mangapapa April 1979, Ruahihi 1981); Trustpower 1994; merger with Tauranga Electricity 31 Oct 1997; bought Coleridge, Highbank/Montalto and Matahina from ECNZ in 1998; bought Waipori, Patea, Paerau, Patearoa, Kumara, Branch and others by March 1999; Cobb from NGC March 2003; Manawa 2022; Contact 11 July 2025.

wp-powerco.title: Powerco
wp-powerco.note: Powerco acquired Egmont Electricity in September 1997; after the 1998 reforms sold its five hydro power stations to TrustPower.

wp-lake-mahinerangi.title: Lake Mahinerangi
wp-lake-mahinerangi.note: Waipori scheme construction from 1903, power from 27 April 1907; Mahinerangi dam 1927–31, raised to 33.5 m by 1946; four dams and stations.

mfe-wairau-2009.title: The TrustPower Wairau River hydro power proposal: a review of the processing of the resource consent applications, 5: The environmental setting (October 2009)
mfe-wairau-2009.note: TrustPower bought the Branch Scheme from Marlborough Electric in 1998, after the reforms separated generation from distribution.

comcom-cobb-2009.title: Energy companies warned over alleged anti-competitive behaviour (24 November 2009)
comcom-cobb-2009.note: Cobb was owned by NGC Holdings and sold by tender in 2002; acquired by TrustPower for $92.5 million in 2003.

trustpower-waipori-2007.title: Waipori Centenary Talks Start This Week (31 October 2007)
trustpower-waipori-2007.note: Developed by the Waipori Falls Hydro-Electric Power Company; bought by Dunedin City Council during construction in 1904 for £31,000; first power 1907; the council sold the scheme to TrustPower in 1998 for $70 million.

wd-q5138774.note: Station point (CC0), read 19 Nov 2026; not yet checked against the LINZ aerial.

wd-q131745148.note: Station point (CC0), read 19 Nov 2026; not yet checked against the LINZ aerial.

wd-q6748611.note: Station point (CC0), read 19 Nov 2026; not yet checked against the LINZ aerial.

wd-q123943279.note: Station point (CC0), read 19 Nov 2026; not yet checked against the LINZ aerial.

wd-q7144392.note: Station point (CC0), read 19 Nov 2026; not yet checked against the LINZ aerial.

wd-q140959164.note: Station point (CC0), read 19 Nov 2026; not yet checked against the LINZ aerial.

wd-q61448288.note: Station point (CC0), read 19 Nov 2026; not yet checked against the LINZ aerial.
